source.title_on_document: Can You Make It Sound Like You? Post-Editing LLM-Generated Text for Personal Style

supplement.where: Appendices A-D, PDF pp. 13-29. The main text points to these appendices; no separately missing statistical supplement is identified.
supplement.holds: Appendix A gives recruitment, exclusions, and permutation-test details (pp. 13-14). Appendix B includes examples (Table 1, p. 15), embedding-model validation and robustness (Tables 2-3, p. 16), style-importance mixed-model coefficients/SEs/CIs (Tables 4-6, p. 18), preference rankings (Table 7, p. 19), linguistic acceptability (Figure 12, p. 20), and the acceptability/style-change mixed model (Table 8, p. 21). Appendix C contains the independent formative survey and task counts (pp. 22-24). Appendix D contains the interface and survey screenshots (pp. 24-29).

paper_design_summary: An online within-person experiment analyzed 81 Prolific writers who completed randomized blocks of four AI-draft post-editing tasks and two unassisted writing tasks, with task allocation also randomized (pp. 4-5, section 4; p. 24, Table 9). Automated style embeddings measured personal stylistic alignment and similarity across different writers; exploratory analyses also scored linguistic acceptability (pp. 5-7, sections 5-6; pp. 20-21, Appendix B.7.1). A separate formative survey analyzed 88 Prolific respondents to select writing scenarios and did not involve AI-assisted creative output (pp. 22-23, Appendix C).

studies.label: Main online writing and post-editing experiment

assignment.what_was_assigned: Each participant completed both treatment and control writing blocks. Their order was randomized, as indicated by the randomized-block description and the randomization bracket in Figure 1. Six self-selected tasks were also randomized between conditions: four post-editing tasks and two unassisted tasks (p. 4, section 4 and Figure 1; p. 24, Table 9).
assignment.quote: As illustrated in Figure 1, participants completed pre- and post-surveys, task difficulty surveys, a brief tutorial, and two randomized writing task blocks (treatment and control).
assignment.locator: p. 4, section 4 and Figure 1; p. 24, Table 9 caption
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 1, Introduction, footnote 2: https://aspredicted.org/ck6xk4.pdf; p. 3, section 3. The linked preregistration was not separately retrieved.

arms.name: Post-edited LLM drafts
arms.description: Participants first planned content, then edited a supplied LLM-generated draft to express their personal style. Four tasks per participant; the same analyzed people also completed the control block (pp. 4-5, section 4; p. 24, Table 9).

arms.name: Unassisted human writing
arms.description: Participants planned content and wrote directly from those plans without seeing any LLM-generated text for those tasks. Two tasks per participant; these are the same people as in the treatment block (pp. 4-5, section 4; p. 24, Table 9).

arms.name: LLM-generated drafts before post-editing
arms.description: The original drafts supplied in the treatment tasks, retained as a pre-editing output benchmark. This is not a third randomized participant arm and contributes no additional people (p. 5, sections 4-6; pp. 6-7, Figures 3-6).

participants.exclusions: The paper reports 100 recruited and 81 included in the final analysis. Under preregistered criteria, it discarded responses from people who never edited any LLM-generated draft or did not complete the entire study. It does not give a count specifically at randomization or counts for each exclusion reason. The recruitment target was reduced for completion-time/payment-budget reasons, not based on results (p. 13, Appendix A.1 and footnote 13).
participants.who: English-fluent Prolific users, limited to one session per person (p. 13, Appendix A.1). The same 81 analyzed writers contribute to both conditions; arm counts must not be added.
participants.quote: Following our preregistered exclusion criteria, we discarded responses where participants never edited any of the LLM-generated drafts or did not complete the entire study, leaving 81 participants.
participants.locator: p. 4, section 4; p. 13, Appendix A.1; p. 24, Table 9 caption

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-o4-mini (OpenAI, 2025), as named on p. 5, section 5.1
ai_tool.how_used: A task-specific prompt combines the writing scenario and the participant’s planned bullet-point details to generate an initial draft. Participants receive that draft and edit it themselves; the model does not edit their own draft. Draft generation and example prompt are described on p. 5, sections 4 and 5.1. The role code denotes supplied generated content (full drafts).

task.description: Participants selected six of eight personal writing scenarios: thank-you letter, apology letter, wedding or birthday speech, catch-up letter, condolence letter, reassurance/encouragement message, wedding vows, or eulogy/obituary/tribute. Four tasks were assigned to post-editing and two to unassisted writing. They supplied fictional details and aimed to express their own style (pp. 4-5, section 4; p. 24, Table 9 and Appendix D).
task.duration: At least two minutes per treatment post-editing task (p. 5, section 4); mean total study completion time 1.69 hours (p. 13, Appendix A.1). No separate total writing-block time is stated.

outcomes.name: Between-participant stylistic diversity / homogeneity (H2a and H2b)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity of LUAR-MUD style embeddings between texts from different participants; higher similarity means greater homogeneity and lower diversity (pp. 5-7, sections 5.2 and 6.2, Figure 6). H2a compares post-edited writing with unassisted writing; H2b uses the original LLM drafts as a second benchmark, not an independently assigned group. CISR is an alternative embedding-model robustness check of the same outcome (pp. 14-16, Appendix B.2, Table 3). No numerical arm means, SDs, or exact pair counts are printed. H2 is one of the paper’s two main preregistered hypotheses (p. 3, section 3).

contrasts.reported: H2a, LUAR-MUD: p = 0.0002, g = 1.42, 95% CI [1.33, 1.51]. CISR robustness: p = 0.0002, g = 1.03, 95% CI [0.91, 1.14]. Positive printed g denotes higher similarity (lower diversity) in post-edited text. Direction is coded for diversity; the printed effect has not been re-signed.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, section 6.2; p. 7, Figure 6; p. 16, Table 3, H2a

contrasts.reported: H2b, LUAR-MUD: p = 0.0002, g = -0.69, 95% CI [-0.74, -0.63]. CISR robustness: p = 0.0002, g = -0.66, 95% CI [-0.70, -0.62]. Negative printed g denotes lower similarity (higher diversity) after post-editing. Direction is coded for diversity; the printed effect has not been re-signed.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, section 6.2; p. 7, Figure 6; p. 16, Table 3, H2b

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine similarity of style embeddings; lower similarity means more diversity.
diversity_detail.embedding_model: LUAR-MUD (Rivera-Soto et al., 2021); robustness with CISR (Wegmann et al., 2022).
diversity_detail.computed_over: Pairs of texts from different participants, separately within the unassisted human, post-edited, and original LLM-generated sets (p. 7, Figure 6). The PDF does not explicitly state whether all possible pairs are used or give their number. Appendix A.2 (pp. 13-14) describes matching reference tasks where applicable.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Two-tailed permutation tests with 10,000 permutations (p. 13, Appendix A.2); Hedges’ g and 95% confidence intervals from 1000 bootstrap samples (p. 5, section 6). Raw p-values are reported; preregistered significance claims use Benjamini-Hochberg correction at q = 0.05. The PDF does not specify whether resampling preserves participant clusters or dependence between pairs sharing a writer.
diversity_detail.notes: H2a supports eligibility. Both human conditions use the same writers, not independent groups. Diversity directions are opposite to printed similarity-effect signs. The distribution is shown in Figure 6; no values have been estimated from the plot.

outcomes.name: Similarity to other participants’ post-edited writing versus own unassisted writing (H2c)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Diagnostic of shared post-edited style: the same post-edited texts are compared with other participants’ post-edited texts and with the author’s own unassisted control writing. This changes the reference source, not randomized treatment assignment (p. 6, section 6.2 and Figure 5 right). CISR is a robustness variant (p. 16, Table 3).

contrasts.treatment_arm: Post-edited LLM drafts (reference: other participants’ post-edited text)
contrasts.control_arm: Post-edited LLM drafts (reference: own unassisted text)
contrasts.reported: H2c, LUAR-MUD: p = 0.0002, g = 1.14, 95% CI [1.02, 1.26]. CISR: p = 0.0002, g = 2.09, 95% CI [1.94, 2.24]. Post-edited text is more similar to other people’s post-edited text than to its author’s control text. The direction field indicates greater homogenization / lower stylistic distinctiveness; printed g is retained on the similarity scale.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, section 6.2 and Figure 5 right; p. 16, Table 3, H2c

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine stylistic similarity, contrasting an other-writer post-edited reference with an own-writer unassisted reference.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Post-edited treatment texts versus other participants’ post-edited texts and versus the same writer’s unassisted reference texts (p. 6, Figure 5 right). Appendix A.2 describes concatenated own-control reference texts; the exact aggregation over other-writer references and number of observations are not specified.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Two-tailed permutation tests with 10,000 permutations (p. 13, Appendix A.2); Hedges’ g and 95% confidence intervals from 1000 bootstrap samples (p. 5, section 6). Raw p-values are reported; preregistered significance claims use Benjamini-Hochberg correction at q = 0.05. The PDF does not specify whether resampling preserves participant clusters or dependence between pairs sharing a writer.
diversity_detail.notes: This is a reference-source diagnostic, not an additional randomized AI-versus-no-AI estimate. Similarity and diversity directions are opposite.

outcomes.name: Stylistic similarity to the author’s own unassisted writing (H1a)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Stylistic authenticity/self-similarity, not a creativity rating or within-person idea flexibility. Each treatment text before and after editing is compared with an embedding of that participant’s concatenated control texts (p. 13, Appendix A.2). CISR is a robustness variant (p. 16, Table 3). Exploratory mixed models examine style importance (pp. 18-19, Table 4) and changes in linguistic acceptability (p. 21, Table 8); these are variants of the same output outcome. Appendix B.4 (pp. 17-18) additionally compares initial self-similarity across demographic subgroups and reports disagreement between embedding models. Appendix B.7.3 (p. 22) relates self-similarity change to the number, length, and total character volume of edits; these are associations, not additional assigned arms.

contrasts.reported: H1a, LUAR-MUD: p = 0.0002, g = 0.55, 95% CI [0.38, 0.71]. CISR: p = 0.0002, g = 0.48, 95% CI [0.32, 0.64]. Table 4 exploratory post-edited (True): Estimate = 0.055, SE = 0.006, z = 9.167, p < .001, 95% CI [0.043, 0.066]; post-edited (True) x personal style importance (Non-max): Estimate = -0.017, SE = 0.013, z = -1.280, p = .201, 95% CI [-0.042, 0.009].
contrasts.locator: p. 5, section 6.1; p. 6, Figure 3 right; p. 16, Table 3, H1a; p. 18, Table 4; p. 19, Appendix B.5

outcomes.name: Individuality of stylistic alignment: own versus other participants’ unassisted reference text (H1a′)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Personal stylistic alignment, comparing resemblance to the writer’s own control style with resemblance to other people’s control styles. The paper discusses this as evidence that post-editing adds individually characteristic features rather than generic human features (p. 6, section 6.1 and Figure 5 left). It is kept distinct from the condition-level diversity outcome. CISR robustness is in Table 3; the exploratory reference-author and CoLA model in Table 8 uses changes in this similarity outcome. The H1a′ prose discusses stylistic shifts, whereas Figure 5 left plots post-editing levels; the precise statistic’s construction merits checking in the released analysis.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Post-edited LLM drafts (reference: other participants’ unassisted text)
contrasts.control_arm: Post-edited LLM drafts (reference: own unassisted text)
contrasts.reported: H1a′, LUAR-MUD: p = 0.0002, g = -0.56, 95% CI [-0.70, -0.43]. CISR: p = 0.0002, g = -0.30, 95% CI [-0.44, -0.16]. Figure 5 left and the text indicate greater resemblance to one’s own than to other participants’ control writing. Table 8 exploratory change-score model: reference author (self), Estimate = 0.027, SE = 0.004, z = 6.079, p < .001, 95% CI [0.018, 0.035]; CoLA difference, Estimate = -0.086, SE = 0.031, z = -2.777, p = .005, 95% CI [-0.147, -0.025]; CoLA difference x reference author (self), Estimate = -0.116, SE = 0.040, z = -2.931, p = .003, 95% CI [-0.193, -0.038].
contrasts.locator: p. 6, section 6.1 and Figure 5 left; p. 16, Table 3, H1a′; p. 21, Table 8 and Appendix B.7.1

outcomes.name: Stylistic similarity to LLM-generated writing / AI-likeness (H1b)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: LUAR-MUD cosine similarity to LLM-generated reference texts before versus after human post-editing (pp. 5-6, sections 5.2 and 6.1, Figure 3 left). CISR embeddings and Pangram AI-authorship likelihood are alternative measures of the same H1b claim and are grouped here as robustness variants (p. 16, Table 3). The primary embedding comparison involves text-reference pairs; Pangram instead scores individual outputs. Task-matched reference selection is described in Appendix A.2 (pp. 13-14); full aggregation details and observation counts are not given. Table 5 (p. 18) is an exploratory moderation analysis by perceived style importance. These scores do not by themselves measure creativity or diversity across people.

contrasts.locator: p. 5, section 6.1; p. 6, Figure 3 left; p. 16, Table 3, H1b; p. 18, Table 5; p. 19, Appendix B.5

outcomes.name: Post-edited text’s similarity to own unassisted style versus LLM style (H1c)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: For the same post-edited text, compares similarity to the author’s control writing with similarity to LLM-generated reference writing (p. 6, section 6.1 and Figure 4 right). This tests residual model style; it is not a comparison of separate groups of participants. CISR is a robustness variant (p. 16, Table 3); Table 6 (pp. 18-19) is an exploratory style-importance moderation model of this reference-source contrast.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Post-edited LLM drafts (reference: own unassisted text)
contrasts.reported: H1c, LUAR-MUD: p = 0.0002, g = -1.43, 95% CI [-1.55, -1.32]. CISR: p = 0.0002, g = -2.30, 95% CI [-2.46, -2.15]. Post-edited text remains more similar to LLM writing than to the author’s control writing. Table 6 exploratory same-participant (True): Estimate = -0.125, SE = 0.005, z = -25.670, p < .001, 95% CI [-0.135, -0.116]; same-participant (True) x personal style importance (Non-max): Estimate = -0.053, SE = 0.011, z = -4.977, p < .001, 95% CI [-0.073, -0.032].
contrasts.locator: p. 6, section 6.1 and Figure 4 right; p. 16, Table 3, H1c; p. 18, Table 6; p. 19, Appendix B.5

outcomes.name: Linguistic acceptability of the final writing (CoLA score)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Exploratory linguistic acceptability judgments for original LLM, post-edited, and unassisted texts using a model from Morris et al. (2020) fine-tuned on expert judgments from the Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability (Warstadt et al., 2019). Higher score means more linguistically acceptable. This is output-level language quality, not a creativity rating. The relationship of acceptability changes to stylistic alignment is a secondary analysis of outcomes S1-O3/S1-O4 (pp. 20-21, Appendix B.7.1, Figure 12 and Table 8).

contrasts.reported: The text states that post-edited writing is more linguistically acceptable than fully human-authored control text: p < .0001, g = -1.29, 95% CI [-1.57, -1.05]. The printed g sign is retained even though it is opposite to the treatment-minus-control direction used in this form; direction follows the prose and Figure 12.

The text states that post-edited writing is less linguistically acceptable than the original LLM-generated text: p < .0001, g = 0.59, 95% CI [0.45, 0.73]. The printed g sign is retained; direction follows the prose and Figure 12.

studies.label: Separate formative survey selecting personally meaningful writing scenarios

assignment.what_was_assigned: Only the presentation order of candidate writing scenarios was randomized. There was no assignment to AI assistance, no AI condition, and no scored writing task (pp. 22-23, Appendix C).
assignment.quote: These tasks were shown to participants in a randomized order.

arms.name: Formative scenario-selection survey
arms.description: All respondents selected scenarios where personal style matters; this was used to choose tasks for the main study (pp. 22-23, Appendix C).

participants.exclusions: 102 people completed the formative survey; 88 passed its attention checks and form the reported analysis sample. The paper does not report a randomization-stage count (p. 23, Appendix C).
participants.who: Prolific participants who were not allowed to participate in the main study (p. 23, Appendix C).
participants.quote: 102 participants completed this formative survey of which 88 passed the attention checks.

ai_tool.how_used: No AI assistance was used in this formative scenario-selection survey (pp. 22-23, Appendix C).

task.description: From fifteen candidate writing scenarios plus two attention-check scenarios, participants selected eight options: six real scenarios and the two checks. No creative output was produced or scored. The authors used the preferences to select the eight main-study scenarios (pp. 22-23, Appendix C).
task.duration: Median completion time 3.53 minutes (p. 23, Appendix C).

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: No reuse of another paper’s participants is stated. The main experiment and formative survey explicitly used non-overlapping samples.
sample_overlap.quote: Formative study participants were also recruited from Prolific, and were not allowed to also complete the main study.

company_involvement.description: Pangram provided API credits. All listed authors are affiliated with the University of Maryland; the acknowledgment also lists public research funding. Use of OpenAI models alone is not treated as evidence of OpenAI sponsorship.

eligibility.reason: S1 qualifies: people completed both AI-assisted and unassisted writing under randomized block order, with tasks randomized between the conditions (p. 4, section 4 and Figure 1; p. 24, Table 9). There were 81 people analyzed, above the 50-person threshold (p. 13, Appendix A.1); this is not a count of ideas or texts. H2a measures stylistic similarity across different writers’ actual outputs using embeddings (p. 6, section 6.2; p. 7, Figure 6; p. 16, Table 3), satisfying the codebook’s inclusion of writing tasks with across-writer similarity outcomes. Participants received generated drafts as assistance, so the main design is not ai_vs_human. S2 is a separate formative survey with no scored creative output and is not the study supporting eligibility.

one_line_finding: Among 81 analyzed writers, post-edited AI drafts were less stylistically diverse than unassisted writing (H2a similarity g = 1.42, 95% CI [1.33, 1.51], p = .0002; p. 6, section 6.2; p. 16, Table 3).
open_questions: The paper gives recruitment counts but not counts specifically at random assignment; the main-study n_randomized is therefore null (pp. 4 and 13).

For the embedding comparisons, does the released analysis average over reference texts before testing, and do permutation/bootstrap samples preserve participant clusters and shared-writer dependence in text pairs? The PDF does not fully specify this (p. 5, section 6; pp. 13-14, Appendix A.2).

The H1a′ prose discusses differential stylistic changes, whereas Figure 5 left shows post-editing levels. Confirm which quantity the Table 3 effect standardizes before extracting an estimate (p. 6; p. 16).

The CoLA effects are printed with signs opposite to the treatment-minus-benchmark direction implied by the prose; retain the printed values and verify the contrast orientation during extraction (pp. 20-21, Figure 12 and Appendix B.7.1).
notes: All 805 lines of the markdown conversion were read, including references and appendices; the PDF tables, figures, appendices, and image-only interface pages were inspected. Locators use PDF page numbers. The saved PDF itself identifies arXiv v1; candidate search notes and later-version status were not treated as verified evidence. The paper calls H1 and H2 its two main preregistered hypotheses (p. 3); related objective outcomes are marked paper_primary, without claiming that an independently inspected preregistration designated one unique primary endpoint. H2a is the preferred across_people contrast under the codebook. Outcome inventory from tables/figures and appendices: Figures 3-5 and Table 3 report self-similarity, similarity to others’ unassisted writing, similarity to LLM writing (also Pangram detection), the LLM-versus-self reference gap, and the other-post-edited-versus-self gap. Figure 6/Table 3 report between-writer homogeneity for post-edited versus unassisted and raw LLM text. Figures 7-9 report perceived stylistic authenticity, its correlation with automatic self-similarity, and perceived usability; these are self-reports/validation and are not counted as objective creativity outcomes. Figure 10 reports identity-expression preferences. Table 7/Figure 11 report ranked reasons for preferred future writing mode, including originality; these are not originality scores on independently evaluated outputs. Figure 12 reports linguistic acceptability, retained as S1-O7. Tables 4-6 and 8 are alternative/conditional analyses of the already-listed stylistic outcomes. Table 2 reports authorship-model validation (mean reciprocal rank and recall), not a treatment effect on creativity. Table 1 provides individual examples of stylistic changes, detector-score changes, and word error rate, not additional population-level outcomes. The descriptive lexical/edit-mechanism analyses in Appendix B.7 are inventoried but not counted as separate creativity or diversity outcomes: contraction frequency, LLM-associated word frequencies, em-dash removal, counts of edited spans, edited-span length, and changed-character volume (pp. 21-22). These characterize editing operations or selected lexical features, rather than output novelty, creativity, or across-writer diversity. Their relations to self-similarity are supporting analyses of S1-O3. Appendix B.1 checks within/between-writer consistency of initial model generations as a design validation (p. 14). Figures 14-15 report formative scenario choices/coverage and main-study perceived style importance; Table 9 reports task observation counts. Figures 1-2 and 16-21 show procedure/interface rather than additional scored output outcomes. No relevant objective creativity/diversity outcome was omitted because of the fifteen-outcome cap. Post-editing is part of producing the AI-assisted output while the supplied AI draft remains available; it is not an after_ai test merely because generation precedes human editing. The unassisted tasks are randomized control blocks, and no separate post-removal or delayed effect is reported. All timing is immediate/same-session (pp. 4-5). The study count includes the independent formative survey (S2), so the largest single analyzed sample in the final summary is 88 even though the eligible writing experiment has 81. Main-study arm counts refer to the same people. No output/pair sample size has been inferred from task counts. The original LLM drafts are listed only as an output benchmark, not as an extra randomized human group. Country is not stated. The data link is explicitly given on p. 1, footnote 4, and p. 15, Table 1 caption. A separate code-availability statement was not confirmed, so code_url is blank. All effect sizes and intervals are transcribed, not computed; no standard errors were derived. H2 directions are expressed as diversity while printed numerical effects remain on the similarity scale. Participant clustering/random-effects specifications and standardization details are insufficiently documented for assuming that the printed precision is suitable for pooling; this does not alter the screening eligibility decision.
